topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Sorting is not one operation with one universal implementation. HarborWorks may sort a handful of already-nearly-ordered readings, merge large ordered batches, or reorder a duplicate-heavy event stream. Input distribution, memory budget, stability, and worst-case requirements all affect the choice.

blocks.text: HarborWorks needs a sorted report, but several implementations can satisfy that requirement with different costs, storage needs, and tie behavior. An insertion sort can be attractive for a small nearly ordered batch, a merge process can preserve equal-key order, and a partitioning sort can avoid a full auxiliary value buffer. None of those advantages is a universal verdict.

topics.title: 16.1 Understanding Elementary Sorting Algorithms
topics.summary: Elementary sorts expose the decisions hidden inside a sorting interface. They are useful learning tools and can be practical for small ranges. Their simplicity does not make their costs interchangeable: insertion sort responds to existing order, while selection sort keeps scanning for a minimum.

blocks.text: The comparison uses strict less-than, so a value is not shifted past an equal predecessor. This makes the algorithm stable when generalized to records under a consistent comparator: equal-key records retain their input order. blocks.text: Selection sort maintains a prefix of final smallest elements. At each position i, scan the remaining suffix for its smallest value and exchange it with the value at i. An exchange can move a record across another equal-key record, so this implementation is not stable. Selection uses relatively few swaps but still performs the full suffix scans.

blocks.text: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. At iteration i, save the next value, shift larger prefix values one position right, and place the saved value in the resulting gap. The prefix grows by one while the suffix remains unprocessed. This is a direct loop-invariant design rather than repeated global searching for order.

topics.title: 16.1.2 Understanding Quadratic Complexity
topics.summary: Selection sort performs roughly n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of existing order, giving quadratic time. Insertion sort has the same worst-case growth when values arrive in reverse order, but an already sorted input requires only one failed shift comparison per insertion and therefore linear work.

blocks.text: Counting comparisons and movements can be more illuminating than wall-clock timing at this stage. blocks.text: Selection sort scans suffixes of lengths n, n-1, and so on to find successive minima. Ignoring a constant convention about the current candidate, the number of comparisons follows a triangular sum and is quadratic. Already sorted input does not eliminate those scans in this implementation.

blocks.text: Insertion sort’s work depends more strongly on disorder. On an already sorted sequence, each next value needs only the failed comparison that confirms its position. On reverse order, each inserted value can shift the entire prefix, producing a quadratic total. The number of inversions helps explain movement: each shift removes one out-of-order pair for this scalar algorithm.

blocks.text: An inversion is a pair of positions i < j whose values are out of the requested order. A nearly ordered sequence can have few inversions even when its length is moderately large. That observation provides a more precise workload description than the vague phrase “almost sorted.” It also suggests generated fixtures with controlled local swaps rather than only fully sorted and fully reversed extremes.

blocks.text: Complexity counts should distinguish comparisons from moves. Selection sort can perform quadratic comparisons while using only a linear number of final swaps. Insertion sort can perform many shifts. If comparison is expensive and movement cheap, the tradeoff differs from a workload with cheap integer comparison and large objects. One scalar wall-clock number hides those mechanisms.

blocks.text: Quadratic growth can still be acceptable under a deliberate small bound. If a component sorts at most sixteen entries, a simple implementation may be easier to verify than a more complex one. The bound must be enforced or maintained, not merely assumed from today’s input. A future change from sixteen to sixteen thousand alters the engineering decision.

topics.title: 16.2 Understanding Efficient Sorting Algorithms
topics.summary: Efficient comparison sorts reduce the amount of repeated searching. Merge sort combines already-sorted subranges. Quick sort partitions around a pivot so later work can focus on independent sides. Their extra-memory, stability, and worst-case properties differ.

topics.title: 16.2.1 Implementing Merge Sort
topics.summary: Merge sort divides a half-open range into two smaller ranges until each has at most one element. After recursively sorting both halves, merge them by repeatedly selecting the smaller remaining front value. Every selected value is the smallest still available across both sorted halves, which proves the output prefix remains sorted.

blocks.text: When keys are equal, the code selects from the left half. That tie rule preserves stability across the split. A reusable temporary vector is allocated once outside recursion; each merge writes its range into the temporary storage and copies it back. The implementation uses O(n) auxiliary element storage and O(log n) call depth.

The implementation uses O(n) auxiliary element storage and O(log n) call depth.

blocks.text: At each recursion level the total merge work is O(n), and there are O(log n) levels, giving O(n log n) time. Empty and one-element ranges return immediately. Allocation failure occurs before any sorting mutation in the wrapper because the temporary vector is constructed first. This integer implementation has simpler movement behavior than a fully generic merge sort over throwing element types.

blocks.text: Merge sort divides a range into two smaller ranges, sorts both, then combines their ordered outputs. The merge step repeatedly selects the next smaller front value from the two remaining subranges. Each output position is filled once, and each input position advances at most once during that merge.

blocks.text: The dependency structure is important. Merging assumes both halves are already sorted under the same comparator. Calling the merge routine on arbitrary halves does not establish a sorted result. The recursive split reaches empty or one-element ranges, which are sorted without work, and then builds larger sorted ranges upward.

blocks.text: The example allocates one temporary vector for the entire sort and reuses its indexed regions. It does not allocate a new buffer at every recursive call. This keeps auxiliary value storage linear, while recursive call depth is logarithmic for the balanced splits. Output is copied back into the original range after each merge.

blocks.text: On equivalent values, the comparison chooses the left side first. For tagged records, that policy preserves relative order across the two halves when each half is itself stably sorted. Stability follows inductively through the merge tree. Choosing the right on equality would still sort keys but could reorder equal-key records.

Exhaustion branches are not incidental edge handling; they are part of the proof that every output position receives a valid remaining value.

reading.title: 16.2.1 Implementing Merge Sort
paragraphs: Merge sort divides a half-open range into two smaller ranges until each has at most one element. After recursively sorting both halves, merge them by repeatedly selecting the smaller remaining front value. Every selected value is the smallest still available across both sorted halves, which proves the output prefix remains sorted.

When keys are equal, the code selects from the left half. That tie rule preserves stability across the split. A reusable temporary vector is allocated once outside recursion; each merge writes its range into the temporary storage and copies it back. The implementation uses O(n) auxiliary element storage and O(log n) call depth.

At each recursion level the total merge work is O(n), and there are O(log n) levels, giving O(n log n) time. Empty and one-element ranges return immediately. Allocation failure occurs before any sorting mutation in the wrapper because the temporary vector is constructed first. This integer implementation has simpler movement behavior than a fully generic merge sort over throwing element types.

Merge sort divides a range into two smaller ranges, sorts both, then combines their ordered outputs. The merge step repeatedly selects the next smaller front value from the two remaining subranges. Each output position is filled once, and each input position advances at most once during that merge.

The dependency structure is important. Merging assumes both halves are already sorted under the same comparator. Calling the merge routine on arbitrary halves does not establish a sorted result. The recursive split reaches empty or one-element ranges, which are sorted without work, and then builds larger sorted ranges upward.

The example allocates one temporary vector for the entire sort and reuses its indexed regions. It does not allocate a new buffer at every recursive call. This keeps auxiliary value storage linear, while recursive call depth is logarithmic for the balanced splits. Output is copied back into the original range after each merge.

On equivalent values, the comparison chooses the left side first. For tagged records, that policy preserves relative order across the two halves when each half is itself stably sorted. Stability follows inductively through the merge tree. Choosing the right on equality would still sort keys but could reorder equal-key records.

The midpoint uses the same safe interval style as binary search. The base condition checks range length before recursion. The merge loop checks whether either half is exhausted before reading it. Exhaustion branches are not incidental edge handling; they are part of the proof that every output position receives a valid remaining value.

The O(n log n) comparison/work model comes from logarithmically many balanced merge levels with linear combined work per level. That model does not include arbitrary costs hidden in a custom comparator or element move. The example’s integer contract keeps those operations simple enough to make the structural argument visible.

Allocation failure before mutation leaves the original vector untouched in this implementation. A generic merge whose element assignments can throw during later stages needs a separate partial-mutation guarantee; one temporary allocation does not automatically make the entire operation transactional.

topics.title: Review answers and solution notes
topics.summary: Insertion’s shift count is near zero for sorted data and quadratic for reversed data. Selection still scans every suffix in both cases. Stability means original positions increase within each equal-key group after sorting. The smaller-side recursion strategy bounds nested call depth but does not eliminate highly unbalanced repeated partition work; a low depth reading alone is not evidence of fast sorting.

blocks.text: Review reasoning. Why is sortedness alone insufficient? Values can be lost or duplicated. Why does stable merge select the left on equality? It preserves prior cross-half order. Why can selection sort be unstable? A distant swap can cross equal-key records. Why not advance after swapping from quick sort’s greater region? The incoming value is unclassified. Why does smaller-side recursion not guarantee good time complexity? It controls call depth, not pivot balance or total partition work.
